learnings.title: How to Use This Guide
learnings.answer:
This is a field manual, not a tutorial — it assumes you've shipped React and just need the internals, the vocabulary, and the traps organized for interview conditions.

Read the mental-model and deep-dive entries once, start to finish, to rebuild your understanding. Keep the **Gotcha Bank**, **Rapid-Fire Q&A**, and **Cheat Sheet** entries starred for the morning of the interview.

Every deep dive follows the same shape: a plain-English explanation, a way to *see* it, real code (bad vs. good where it matters), the mistakes candidates actually make, and a one-line answer you can say out loud without sounding like you memorized it.

learnings.title: Elements → Fiber → DOM: React's Three Trees
learnings.answer:
React keeps **three** trees, not one. JSX compiles to plain objects (**elements**) that describe *what you want*. React turns those into a **Fiber tree** — a linked list of work units, one per component instance, that also mirrors the real DOM. Only the Fiber tree persists across renders; elements are thrown away every render.

```javascript
Elements (JSX output)      Fiber tree (persists)         DOM
<App />              →    FiberNode{type:App}      →   (no direct node)
  <List items />     →      FiberNode{type:List}   →   <ul>
    <Row key />       →        FiberNode{type:Row}  →     <li>
```

Each Fiber node stores the component's `type`, its current `props`, its hook state (as a linked list), a pointer to its `alternate` (the work-in-progress twin used during a render), and pointers to its child / sibling / return (parent) — that's how React walks the tree without recursion, so it can pause and resume.

## How to answer in the interview

> "React doesn't diff the DOM directly — it diffs Fiber trees, and only flushes the DOM operations that come out of that diff in one commit."

## Key takeaways

- Elements are cheap, throwaway descriptions recreated every render.
- The Fiber tree is the persistent, diffable structure React actually walks.
- Only the diff's output ever touches the real DOM.

learnings.title: The Render → Commit → Effects Pipeline
learnings.answer:
This single sequence resolves more "which hook runs when" questions than anything else:

```javascript
Render (call components, build WIP tree)
  → Reconciliation (diff against last committed tree)
  → Commit (mutate the real DOM)
  → useLayoutEffect (sync, blocks paint)
  → Browser paint
  → useEffect (async, after paint)
```

**Render** can be paused, thrown away, or redone (concurrent features, Strict Mode) — so it must stay pure. **Commit** is synchronous and always runs to completion once started — DOM mutations are never partially applied.

## Key takeaways

- Nothing in render should have a side effect — React may call it more than once.
- `useLayoutEffect` runs before the browser paints; `useEffect` runs after.
- Commit is atomic: either all the DOM mutations for a render happen, or none do.

learnings.title: Reconciliation: Diffing by Heuristic, Not by Tree Edit-Distance
learnings.answer:
A general tree-diff algorithm is `O(n³)`. React makes it `O(n)` with two assumptions that are true almost all the time in UI trees:

| Comparison | What React does |
| --- | --- |
| Different element **type** at a position | Tear down the whole old subtree (unmount), build the new one fresh |
| Same element **type** | Keep the Fiber & DOM node, patch only the changed props |
| List children | Match by `key`, not position — a stable key says "this is the same logical item," even if it moved |

That's the whole reason `key` matters: without it, React falls back to matching by array index, and reordering, inserting, or removing at the front of a list makes it misattribute state to the wrong item — see the Gotcha Bank entry on `key={index}`.

## Key takeaways

- Different type at a position = full tear-down and rebuild of that subtree.
- Same type = props patched in place, DOM node reused.
- `key` gives list items stable identity across renders — it's not just for silencing a warning.

## Going deeper

The *consequences* of these rules are where the real bugs live — conditional branches that silently preserve state, components declared inside components remounting on every render, index keys defeating `React.memo`, and `key` as a deliberate state reset. See [Diffing, Reconciliation, and the Key Attribute](/advanced-react/6).

learnings.title: One-Way Data Flow
learnings.answer:
```javascript
state (owned by a component)
  → passed down as props
    → children render from props
      → child calls a callback prop
        → parent updates its own state
          → re-render flows back down
```

Data only flows down; behavior flows up through callbacks. There is no built-in way for a child to reach up and mutate a parent's state directly — which is exactly why prop drilling, lifting state up, and Context all exist: they're three different answers to "how do two components that don't own each other's state share it?"

## How to answer in the interview

> "Props flow down, events flow up. Anything that looks like two-way binding in React — a controlled input — is really just this loop running on every keystroke."

learnings.title: How useState Actually Works
The Stale Closure Trap
useEffect vs useLayoutEffect
useMemo & useCallback: What They Actually Buy You
learnings.answer:
`useMemo` memoizes a **value**; `useCallback` memoizes a **function reference** — it's literally `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. Neither skips a render on its own. They only pay off in two situations:

- The computation itself is expensive (sorting/filtering thousands of rows) — skip redoing it when the inputs haven't changed.
- The *reference* needs to stay stable because it's a dependency of another hook, or a prop into a `React.memo`'d child.

## Common over-use

`useMemo(() => a + b, [a, b])` for a cheap arithmetic expression costs *more* than it saves — you pay for the dependency comparison and cache storage on every render for a computation that was never expensive. Memoize the ones that show up in a profile, not the ones that look scary.

## Key takeaways

- Both are performance hints, not semantic guarantees.
- Reach for them when a computation is measurably expensive, or a reference must stay stable for memoization/deps elsewhere.
- Don't wrap everything — the shallow-compare and cache-storage overhead is real.

learnings.title: useRef: The Escape Hatch React Can’t See
learnings.answer:
`ref.current` is a plain mutable box that survives re-renders but never triggers one when written to. Two distinct jobs share the same API:

- **DOM refs** — `<input ref={inputRef} />` to imperatively focus, measure, or scroll.
- **Instance variables** — "a value I need across renders, but the UI never depends on it directly" (a timer id, a previous value for comparison, a mutable flag like `hasFetchedRef.current`).

## How to answer in the interview

> "State is for anything the render output depends on; refs are for anything a render needs to remember without caring about it."

## Going deeper

Callback refs, refs to a list of elements, ref cleanup functions, why a ref can't be a dependency, and React 19's `ref`-as-a-prop (which deprecates `forwardRef`): see [Refs: From Storing Data to Imperative API](/advanced-react/9).

learnings.title: useReducer vs useState
learnings.answer:
Same underlying mechanism — `useReducer` is `useState` with the "next state" logic centralized in one pure `(state, action) => newState` function instead of scattered across every event handler.

Reach for it when: the next state depends on several pieces of the previous state together, there are many related actions (form wizard, undo/redo), or you want the update logic testable in isolation from any component.

## Key takeaways

- `useReducer` centralizes transition logic; `useState` scatters it across handlers.
- Prefer it once a component has several related pieces of state that change together.
- The reducer function is pure and trivially unit-testable without rendering anything.

learnings.title: Rules of Hooks — And Why They Exist
Custom Hooks vs. Plain Helper Functions
What Actually Triggers a Re-render
learnings.answer:
A component **re-renders** when React needs to reconcile a new version of its output. Props changing alone does not schedule a render — something upstream must trigger it.

| Triggers a render | Does *not* |
| --- | --- |
| Own state changes (`setState`, `dispatch`) | `ref.current = x` — refs are invisible to the scheduler |
| Parent re-renders (children render too, unless memoized) | Mutating a state object/array in place, same reference |
| A subscribed Context value changes | Parent re-render + `React.memo` child with shallow-equal props |

## How to answer in the interview

> "Props don't cause a re-render — a parent re-rendering does, and the child receives new props as a side effect of that."

## Going deeper

Two structural fixes beat memoization when state sits too high — [moving state down](/advanced-react/1) and [passing children as props](/advanced-react/2), which keeps a subtree's element reference stable so React skips it entirely.

learnings.title: React.memo and the Reference Trap
Virtualizing Big Lists
Code-Splitting with lazy + Suspense
"The App Is Slow" — The Interview Playbook
learnings.answer:
**Profile first, optimize second** — this sentence alone answers half of what the interviewer is listening for.

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Measure — React DevTools Profiler, browser Performance tab |
| 2 | Cut unnecessary renders — `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` |
| 3 | Virtualize long lists |
| 4 | Code-split routes and heavy components |
| 5 | Defer non-urgent work — `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue` |
| 6 | Split and memoize Context providers |
| 7 | (Rare) move heavy computation off the main thread — Web Workers |

## Anti-patterns

Memoizing every component (the shallow-compare overhead can outweigh a cheap render), `useMemo` on a value that changes every render anyway, and putting high-frequency state — scroll position, mouse coordinates, keystrokes — into Context.

learnings.title: Higher-Order Components (HOC)
Render Props
learnings.answer:
```javascript
<DataFetcher url="/api/user">
  {({ data, loading }) => (loading ? <Spinner /> : <Profile user={data} />)}
</DataFetcher>
```

A prop whose value is a function that returns JSX — the component owns the state, the caller owns the rendering. Same problem hooks solve, from before hooks existed; today a custom hook (`const { data, loading } = useDataFetcher(url)`) does the same job with less nesting.

## Going deeper

Render props still beat both hooks and element props in two cases — when the passed-in UI needs the component's own state, and when the logic is tied to a DOM node the component renders. They also silently cost you the children-as-props render bail-out. See [Render Props: Advanced Configuration](/advanced-react/4).

learnings.title: Compound Components
learnings.answer:
A parent implicitly shares state with its children via Context, so the API reads like plain composable markup instead of one component with a dozen props:

```javascript
<Tabs defaultValue="profile">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab value="profile">Profile</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab value="billing">Billing</Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel value="profile">...</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>
```

This is how most headless UI libraries (Radix, React Aria, Headless UI) are built — the parent owns the shared state in Context, each child reads only what it needs. It trades some implicitness for a dramatically nicer call-site API.

learnings.title: Controlled vs. Uncontrolled
learnings.answer:
| Controlled | Uncontrolled |
| --- | --- |
| `value` + `onChange` — React state is the source of truth | `defaultValue`/`ref` — the DOM is the source of truth |
| Validate/format on every keystroke, easy to reset | Less re-rendering, simpler for "just read it on submit" |

## Gotcha

`<input defaultValue="hello" />` is **uncontrolled** — the DOM node owns subsequent changes even though it had an initial value from React. Switching an input from uncontrolled to controlled (or the reverse) mid-lifecycle throws a React warning.

learnings.title: forwardRef & useImperativeHandle
Portals
Error Boundaries
Where State Should Live
learnings.answer:
| Scope | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Local (`useState`/`useReducer`) | Owned and used by one component and its direct children — the default |
| Lifted to a common parent | Two siblings need to stay in sync |
| Context | Low-frequency, cross-cutting data many distant components read — theme, auth, locale |
| External store (Redux/Zustand/Jotai) | Complex, high-frequency, or deeply cross-cutting client state with time-travel/devtools needs |
| Server-state library (React Query/SWR) | Anything that's really a cache of server data — has its own lifecycle (stale, loading, retry) |

## How to answer in the interview

> "I start local and lift only when two components need to share it. I reach for Context for cross-cutting, low-frequency data, and I treat 'data from the server' as a fundamentally different problem from 'UI state' — that's what pushes me toward React Query over stuffing fetched data into Redux."

learnings.title: Server State vs. Client State
learnings.answer:
This distinction is the biggest shift in React data-fetching opinion over the last few years. Client state (a modal's open/closed flag, form input) is owned by the browser session. Server state (a user's profile, a list of orders) is a local *cache* of something that lives elsewhere, can go stale, and can change without your app touching it.

Server-state libraries (React Query, SWR, RTK Query) exist specifically to manage caching, background refetch, retries, and de-duplication — problems a generic store like Redux doesn't solve out of the box.

learnings.title: Context Re-renders — The Problem and the Fixes
CSR / SSR / SSG / ISR
learnings.answer:
| Strategy | Rendered | Freshness | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CSR | Browser, after JS loads | Always client-fresh | Dashboards, authenticated apps |
| SSR | Server, every request | Always fresh | Personalized, SEO-critical dynamic pages |
| SSG | Build time | Stale until rebuild | Blogs, docs, marketing |
| ISR | Build + background revalidate | Stale-while-revalidate | E-commerce, news at CDN scale |

```javascript
CSR:  browser downloads JS → renders empty shell → hydrates
SSR:  server sends full HTML → browser hydrates → interactive
SSG:  HTML pre-built at deploy → CDN serves instantly
ISR:  SSG + periodic background rebuild (e.g. every 60s)
```

Default to SSG/ISR for public content (free CDN scale). Use SSR when data must be per-request — cookies, auth, live inventory. Use CSR for interactive post-login experiences where SEO doesn't matter. **Hydration** is the step that attaches React's event listeners to already-rendered server HTML, making it interactive.

learnings.title: React Server Components, Actions & use()
learnings.answer:
Server Components are a *new axis*, not a replacement for SSR — a component can be marked to run **only on the server**, never shipped to the client as JS at all.

| | Server Component | Client Component |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runs | Server only, zero JS shipped to browser | Server (for SSR) then hydrates and re-runs client-side |
| Can use | Direct DB/filesystem access, async/await at the top of the component | State, effects, browser APIs, event handlers |
| Marked by | Default in a Server Components framework (Next.js App Router) | `"use client"` directive at the top of the file |

**Actions** are server-side functions callable directly from a form or event handler (`"use server"`) without hand-rolling an API route. **The `use()` hook** reads a promise or Context and can be called conditionally — unlike other hooks — because it's designed to unwrap a Suspense-integrated value, most often inside a Server Component or while streaming.

## Mental model

Server Components shrink the client bundle (their code never ships); Suspense streams the resulting HTML in chunks as each part becomes ready, instead of blocking on the slowest data fetch. It's SSR's "wait for everything" problem solved with streaming plus "why ship this JS at all" solved with Server Components.

learnings.title: React 18 Concurrent Features
useTransition vs useDeferredValue
StrictMode's Double-Invoke Behavior
Testing Strategy — Behavior, Not Implementation
learnings.answer:
React Testing Library's guiding principle: *"the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you."* Query by role and visible text, not by CSS class or component internals — a test that queries `getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i })` survives a refactor that renames an internal `handleClick`; a test on implementation details doesn't.

| Layer | Tool | What it buys you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Vitest/Jest on pure helpers & hooks (`renderHook`) | Fast, isolates logic from rendering |
| Component/integration | React Testing Library | Confidence the UI actually works for a user |
| End-to-end | Playwright/Cypress | Confidence the whole system (routing, network, auth) works |

## How to answer in the interview

> "I test behavior through the same interface a user has — roles, labels, visible text — and keep implementation details like internal state or component names out of assertions, so refactors don't break tests that never should have cared."

learnings.title: Accessibility Essentials
learnings.answer:
| Practice | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Semantic HTML first | `<button>`, not `<div onClick>` |
| Labels | `<label htmlFor={id}>` paired with `<input id={id}>` |
| ARIA only when semantics aren't enough | `aria-expanded`, `role="dialog"`, `aria-live` |
| Keyboard navigation | Tab order, Enter/Space to activate, Escape to close |
| Focus management | Move focus into a modal on open, return it on close |

```javascript
function Field({ label }) {
  const id = useId(); // SSR-safe unique id — for htmlFor/aria-*, not list keys
  return (
    <>
      <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>
      <input id={id} />
    </>
  );
}
```

Radix UI, Headless UI, and React Aria bake accessible interaction patterns into unstyled primitives; `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` catches issues at lint time, `jest-axe`/`axe-core` at test time — but nothing replaces actually tabbing through the app and trying it with VoiceOver or NVDA.

learnings.title: Micro-Frontends & Architecture
Gotcha Bank — 15 Rapid Answers
learnings.answer:
The classic footguns, as one-liners. If you can answer all of these cold, you can answer the follow-up that specializes any of them.

**Q: Why does `key={index}` break when a list can reorder, insert, or delete from the middle?**
A: React matches by key across renders — index keys shift when items move, so React reuses the wrong DOM node/state for the wrong logical item (classic symptom: an uncontrolled input shows the previous item's value).

**Q: Why does my component render twice in development but once in production?**
A: StrictMode intentionally double-invokes render and effects in dev to surface impure logic — it's not a bug, and production never does it.

**Q: Three `setCount(count + 1)` calls in one handler — why does count only go up by 1?**
A: All three read the same stale `count` from that render's closure and batch into one update. Use `setCount(c => c + 1)` three times to actually get +3.

**Q: My `useEffect` loops infinitely — what's the usual cause?**
A: The effect sets state that's also in its own dependency array without a guard, or an object/array/function is recreated every render and listed as a dependency, so the dependency "changes" every time by reference.

**Q: `React.memo` isn't preventing re-renders — why?**
A: A prop is a new object, array, or inline arrow function every render, so the shallow-equality check always fails. Stabilize it with `useMemo`/`useCallback`, or pass primitives.

**Q: Why did mutating state directly with `items.push(x); setItems(items)` not trigger a re-render?**
A: React compares state by reference (`Object.is`). The array reference didn't change, so React may bail out. Always create a new reference: `setItems([...items, x])`.

**Q: Setting `ref.current` in an event handler — why doesn't the UI update?**
A: Refs are mutable boxes outside React's render cycle by design — writing to them never schedules a render. Use state for anything the render output depends on.

**Q: Effect cleanup runs with which values — old or new?**
A: The *old* render's closure. On a dependency change React runs the previous effect's cleanup first (with old values), then the new effect (with new values); on unmount, cleanup runs once, with the last render's values.

**Q: "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" — what causes it and how do you fix it?**
A: An async operation (fetch, timer) resolves after the component unmounted and still calls its setter. Fix with an `AbortController` in the effect cleanup, or a mounted-ref guard.

**Q: Why does a Context consumer re-render even though it only reads one field of the value?**
A: Context has no selective subscription — any change to the Provider's `value` re-renders every consumer. Split contexts or select from an external store instead.

**Q: Calling a hook inside an `if` statement — what breaks, exactly?**
A: Hook state is stored by call order/index. A conditional hook shifts every subsequent hook's index between renders, corrupting their state — not just the conditional one's.

**Q: Is it safe to assume `useMemo` never recomputes unless deps change?**
A: No — React may discard a memoized value to reclaim memory (e.g. for offscreen components) and recompute it later. Treat `useMemo` as a performance hint, never as a semantic guarantee.

**Q: Keys must be globally unique — true or false?**
A: False. Keys only need to be unique among siblings in the same array — the same key can appear in a different list elsewhere in the tree with no conflict.

**Q: Does automatic batching in React 18 apply inside a `setTimeout` or a raw promise `.then`?**
A: Yes — that's the change. Pre-18, batching only happened inside React event handlers; React 18's automatic batching extends it to timeouts, promises, and native event handlers too.

**Q: A form input value only updates on the second keystroke — likely cause?**
A: Usually a controlled input whose `value` is derived from state that's set asynchronously or one render behind, or a debounced state update wired to the wrong variable.

learnings.title: Rapid-Fire Q&A
learnings.answer:
Drawn from the quiz bank — read the question, answer in your head, then check.

**Q: After clicking a button that calls `setCount(count+1)` three times in one handler, what is `count`?**
A: 1. All three calls read the same stale `count` (0) from the closure and each set it to 1; React batches into one re-render.

**Q: Effect has `[count]` as a dependency and logs on effect/cleanup — after one click (0→1), what logs?**
A: "cleanup 0", then "effect 1". The previous effect's cleanup runs first with the old closure value, then the new effect runs with the new value.

**Q: Which of these does not cause a re-render: same-value `setState`, parent re-render, changing a `useRef` value, or a Context value changing?**
A: Changing a `useRef` value. Refs are invisible to React's scheduler by design.

**Q: `useEffect(() => { fetchData(); }, [])` — when does `fetchData` run?**
A: Once, after the initial render (mount). An empty dependency array means the effect never re-runs; cleanup fires only on unmount.

**Q: A memoized `Child` receives `data={{ name: "Alice" }}` built inline in `Parent`. Does clicking an unrelated button in `Parent` re-render `Child`?**
A: Yes. The object literal is a new reference every render, so `React.memo`'s shallow comparison fails. Fix with `useMemo`.

**Q: `<input defaultValue="hello" />` — controlled or uncontrolled?**
A: Uncontrolled. `defaultValue` only sets the initial DOM value; the DOM owns subsequent changes. Controlled inputs use `value` + `onChange`.

**Q: What do error boundaries catch?**
A: Rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors of descendant components — only. Not event handlers, not async code; those still need try/catch.

**Q: A component uses `createPortal` to render into a different DOM node. Do click events still bubble to the logical React parent?**
A: Yes. Events bubble through the React component tree, not the physical DOM tree — a portal only changes where the DOM node lives, not the tree relationship.

**Q: Correct statement about `useLayoutEffect` vs `useEffect`?**
A: `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after DOM mutations, before paint; `useEffect` runs asynchronously after paint.

**Q: Only `theme` changes in a Context whose value is `{ user, theme }` — does a component that only reads `user` re-render?**
A: Yes. Any Provider value change re-renders every consumer — Context has no selective subscription.

**Q: A list uses `key={index}` with uncontrolled inputs. What happens when the first item is removed?**
A: The remaining inputs show mismatched values. Index keys shift, so key 0 now maps to a different logical item, but the DOM node (and its uncontrolled value) is reused as-is.

**Q: In a `Suspense`-wrapped `React.lazy` component, when does the fallback show?**
A: While the lazy component's module is downloading — the dynamic `import()` promise is pending, not while it's rendering.

**Q: What does `startTransition` actually do?**
A: Marks the state update inside it as non-urgent/interruptible — React can pause it to keep a more urgent update (like typing) responsive. It does not delay by a timeout or move work to a worker.

**Q: Which is valid: a conditional hook call, a top-level hook call, calling `useState` in a plain function, or calling `useEffect` inside a `forEach`?**
A: A top-level hook call in a component or custom hook. The other three all violate the rules of hooks.

**Q: Why `setItems(items.map(i => i.id === id ? {...i, done: !i.done} : i))` instead of mutating and calling `setItems(items)`?**
A: React compares state by reference. A mutated array keeps the same reference — React may bail out and skip the re-render entirely.

**Q: What is a Server Component allowed to do that a Client Component can't?**
A: Access the database/filesystem directly and ship zero JS to the browser. In exchange it gives up state, effects, and event handlers — those require `"use client"`.

learnings.title: Cheat Sheet
learnings.answer:
One dense pass for the night before.

### Pipeline
- Render (pure, can pause/discard) → Commit (atomic DOM write)
- `useLayoutEffect` — sync, before paint
- Browser paint
- `useEffect` — async, after paint

### Re-render triggers
- Own state / dispatch changes
- Parent re-renders (unless memoized)
- Subscribed Context value changes
- *Not*: ref writes, same-reference mutation

### Performance toolbox
- Measure first — DevTools Profiler
- `React.memo` + stable props (`useMemo`/`useCallback`)
- Virtualize long lists
- Code-split with `lazy` + `Suspense`
- `useTransition` / `useDeferredValue` for non-urgent updates
- Split & memoize Context providers

### Rendering strategies
- CSR — browser renders; SEO-poor, always fresh
- SSR — server, every request; personalized
- SSG — build time; fastest, stalest
- ISR — SSG + background revalidate
- RSC — zero-JS server-only components

### Patterns → when
- Custom hook — share stateful logic
- Compound components — implicit shared state, composable API
- HOC — wrap the returned element itself
- `forwardRef` — parent needs the child's DOM node
- Portal — escape overflow/z-index ancestor
- Error boundary — contain render-time crashes

### Interview soundbites
- "Props don't cause re-renders — parent re-renders do."
- "Hooks are closures over React's internal hook-slot array."
- "Context has no selective subscription."
- "Profile first, optimize second."
- "Render must stay pure — commit is where side effects belong."
